title: Moving an ECS task to Graviton? Check which ECR digest you pinned
summary:
A pull request changes a Linux Fargate task from X86_64 to ARM64. The image field stays exactly as it was, pinned to a SHA-256 digest. The x86 smoke test is green. Would you approve the change?

I would ask to see one piece of output first. If the x86 and Graviton services share an image reference, pin the digest of the manifest list that contains both architectures. An x86 smoke test can pass with either the list digest or the x86 image digest. The difference shows up when the Arm task needs an image of its own.

Which digest did the build give you?

You can try this during a code review using the Amazon Linux 2023 base image. You will need Bash, Docker Buildx, jq, and access to Amazon ECR Public. All the lookups below read registry metadata.

set -o pipefail
repo=public.ecr.aws/amazonlinux/amazonlinux
release_digest=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "$repo:2023" \
  --format '{{json .Manifest}}' | jq -er '.digest')
release_ref="$repo@$release_digest"

docker buildx imagetools inspect "$release_ref"

Look at the top-level Digest: and the two entries under Manifests:. Here is how they fit together in the November 19, 2026 run, with the hashes shortened for readability. The commands keep the full digests. Your hashes can change as AWS updates the 2023 tag.

amazonlinux:2023
└── sha256:3f018977be7a…  manifest list
    ├── sha256:4ea82ab6042d…  linux/amd64
    └── sha256:7d86656c3ef6…  linux/arm64/v8

Follow the branches as if you were the container runtime. Start at 3f018… on Graviton and there is an Arm entry to select. Start at 4ea82… and you have already arrived at the x86 image. That image has no reference back to the list or across to its Arm sibling. This is why two values copied from the same inspection can behave differently in a task definition. Amazon ECR multi-architecture images

Try the digest that passes the x86 smoke test

Take the x86 entry from the list. Then ask the registry for that image's own configuration. Run this in the same shell so release_ref still points to the release you just inspected.

x86_digest=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw "$release_ref" |
  jq -er '.manifests[]
    | select(.platform.os == "linux" and .platform.architecture == "amd64")
    | .digest')

docker buildx imagetools inspect "$repo@$x86_digest" \
  --format '{{json .Image}}' | jq '{os, architecture}'

{
  "os": "linux",
  "architecture": "amd64"
}

That is a perfectly good digest for an x86-only service. The mistake would be passing it from the x86 test job to the deployment job as the digest for both services. A pipeline can make that mistake even when the build produced the Arm image correctly. Docker Buildx image inspection

What actually ran on Graviton?

On November 22, 2026, I tried the manifest-list digest from the tree above on two EC2 instances in Frankfurt. On each host I gave Docker the same digest and let it choose the platform. Inside each container I started a small Python HTTP server with a single /health endpoint. The running container's image ID matched the configuration digest from the corresponding child manifest in ECR.

EC2 host uname -m inside the container Docker health GET /health
t4g.small (Graviton) aarch64 healthy HTTP 200, body ok
t3.small (x86) x86_64 healthy HTTP 200, body ok

Then I stayed on the Graviton host and deliberately selected the x86 child. I chose /bin/true because a successful run exits immediately with code 0.

docker pull --platform linux/amd64 "$repo@$x86_digest"
docker run --rm --network none --read-only --platform linux/amd64 "$repo@$x86_digest" /bin/true

The pull succeeded. The executable failed to start with exec format error, and Docker returned exit code 255. A CI job that only pulled the image would have passed. You may see a different result on a laptop with x86 emulation enabled. Docker multi-platform images and emulation

I ran this test with Docker on EC2. The Fargate task definition below shows how I would carry the same pin into ECS. A Fargate deployment still needs its own smoke test.

What goes in the ECS task definition?

For the Graviton service, these are the two fields I would review together. This fragment uses the Amazon Linux digest from the example so you can trace it back to the tree. In your service, substitute your application's manifest-list reference.

{
  "runtimePlatform": {
    "operatingSystemFamily": "LINUX",
    "cpuArchitecture": "ARM64"
  },
  "containerDefinitions": [
    {
      "name": "app",
      "image": "public.ecr.aws/amazonlinux/amazonlinux@sha256:3f018977be7a3473a0a473ed105b244b8bdec8683ecb24962f675db23017137b"
    }
  ]
}

The x86 service can keep the same image and specify X86_64. That is also the Linux Fargate default when you omit the CPU architecture. If the task includes a log router or another sidecar, inspect its image too. Every container in that Arm task needs a compatible image. ECS Fargate task definition parameters

Catch the x86-only pin before deployment

I would put this check in the job that writes the task definition. Give it the exact reference the job is about to put in image. For a release shared by Linux x86 and Arm services, it should find both entries.

has_both_platforms() {
  docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw "$1" |
    jq -e '
      [.manifests[]? | select(.platform.os == "linux") | .platform.architecture]
      | (index("amd64") != null) and (index("arm64") != null)
    '
}

Try it twice against the same release. The second call deliberately supplies the x86 child digest.

has_both_platforms "$release_ref"        # true   (exit 0)
has_both_platforms "$repo@$x86_digest"   # false  (exit 1)

Back to the pull request. A false result sends me back to the build output to find the parent digest and check whether the release includes Arm. A true result means the registry advertises both images. Pass that exact reference to deployment so a later tag update cannot change what you tested.

Before I approve that pull request, I also want to see the service answer its own health check on Graviton. An Arm image can still contain an x86 binary copied in during the build. The manifest check tells me the release lists an Arm image. Starting the service tells me whether the application inside it runs.

title: Beyond the Scanner: A Practical Guide to Platform Vulnerability Assessment
summary:
Most engineering teams have some form of application security in place: dependency scanning in CI, a SAST tool, maybe a periodic web app pentest. What often gets less structured attention is the layer underneath — the servers, operating systems, middleware, network devices and VPN gateways that the application actually runs on.

That layer is the target of a platform vulnerability assessment: a review of infrastructure components for known vulnerabilities and configuration problems that could lead to unauthorized access, data exposure or service disruption.

This post looks at platform assessment from an engineer's point of view: how to scope it, what the different scan modes actually tell you, why raw scanner output is not a result, and how to turn findings into a sane remediation queue.

⚠️ All commands below are illustrative. Only scan systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test, and coordinate with whoever operates the environment. Scanning production can generate load and side effects.

Platform vs. web application assessment

These two are often confused, but they look at different layers:

Platform assessment Web application assessment
Targets Servers, OS, middleware, network devices Websites, web apps, related APIs
Looks for Vulnerable software versions, misconfiguration, unnecessary services Authn/authz flaws, input handling, session management
Typical issues Unpatched OS, exposed admin ports, weak device config SQL injection, XSS, broken access control

A web app pentest can come back clean while the web server underneath runs an end-of-life OS with a management port open to the internet. Real systems carry both kinds of risk, so the two assessments are complementary rather than interchangeable.

What a platform assessment typically covers

A reasonable baseline checklist across seven areas:

  1. OS / software — versions, known vulnerabilities, vendor support status
  2. Middleware — web servers, databases: configuration and version
  3. Ports / services — what is listening and reachable, and whether it should be
  4. Authentication / access control — admin accounts, auth methods, privilege scope
  5. Network configuration — firewall rules, ACLs, traffic paths
  6. Encryption / transport — TLS configuration, certificates, cipher suites
  7. Security settings — default configs, unused features, exposed management interfaces

Exact coverage depends on the target, the method and the provider, which is why scoping matters more than tool choice.

Scoping: four decisions that define what you'll learn

1. External vs. internal vantage point

  • External scans hit your systems from the internet. They answer: what does an outside attacker see? — exposed ports, services, version banners, known vulnerabilities.
  • Internal scans run from inside the network. They answer: what happens after the perimeter is breached? — including servers and devices that are not reachable from outside. They require a scanning foothold and network access arranged in advance.

2. Authenticated vs. unauthenticated

  • Unauthenticated scans infer state from network responses only. Closer to the attacker's view, but limited.
  • Authenticated scans log in with an appropriately privileged account and can inspect installed packages and patch levels directly. More accurate for "are we patched?", but they need credential handling and more setup.

3. Automated vs. manual verification

Automated tools are good at breadth: many hosts, many known CVEs, quickly. They also produce false positives (and miss things). Manual verification of significant findings is what turns a list of possible issues into a list of confirmed risks.

4. Environment and conditions

Production or staging? What time window? Which hosts and services are out of scope? Write this down before anyone runs a scan — especially for production, where scanning can add load.

What the first pass looks like (illustrative)

A very first external look at a single host you own might be as simple as:

# Service/version detection on common ports (authorized targets only)
nmap -sV --top-ports 1000 -oA scan/web01-external web01.example.com

And checking what TLS a public endpoint actually negotiates:

# Inspect certificate and negotiated protocol/cipher
openssl s_client -connect web01.example.com:443 -servername web01.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

# Does it still accept TLS 1.0? (expect a handshake failure if disabled)
openssl s_client -connect web01.example.com:443 -tls1 </dev/null

Note what these do not tell you: whether an exposed service is actually exploitable, whether a version banner is accurate (backported patches are common on Linux distributions), or whether firewall rules intended for one segment leak into another. That is where authenticated checks and manual analysis come in.

The real work: triage

The output of a scanner is input, not a result. A useful assessment process looks like this:

  1. Define targets and scope (hosts, IPs, environments, external/internal)
  2. Agree on conditions (timing, access method, exclusions)
  3. Run the assessment (ports/services, known vulns, configuration checks, authenticated scans and manual verification where needed)
  4. Analyze and assess risk (severity, impact, exploitability)
  5. Report with concrete remediation
  6. Fix and re-test

Step 4 is where teams most often go wrong, usually by sorting the spreadsheet by CVSS score and starting from the top.

CVSS is a starting point, not a priority

CVSS gives a standardized severity score for a vulnerability. It does not know whether your vulnerable host is internet-facing, whether the flaw is being exploited in the wild, or whether the box holds customer data or a test fixture.

A simple way to make that context explicit is to combine severity with environmental factors. A sketch:

# Illustrative triage helper -- tune the weights to your environment.
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Finding:
    host: str
    cve: str
    cvss: float              # base score from the advisory
    internet_facing: bool
    known_exploited: bool    # e.g. listed in a known-exploited catalog
    business_critical: bool

def priority(f: Finding) -> float:
    score = f.cvss
    if f.internet_facing:
        score += 2.0
    if f.known_exploited:
        score += 3.0
    if f.business_critical:
        score += 1.5
    return score

findings = [
    Finding("vpn-gw-01", "CVE-XXXX-AAAA", 7.5, True, True, True),
    Finding("build-02", "CVE-XXXX-BBBB", 9.1, False, False, False),
]

for f in sorted(findings, key=priority, reverse=True):
    print(f"{priority(f):5.1f}  {f.host:<10} {f.cve}")

With this, the 7.5 on the internet-facing VPN gateway correctly outranks the 9.1 on an isolated build box. The exact weights matter far less than the habit of asking "exposed? exploited? important?" for every finding.

When you can't patch immediately

Not everything can be fixed this sprint. Legacy dependencies, vendor appliances and change freezes are real. Interim mitigations are legitimate and should be tracked as such:

  • Restrict access to the vulnerable service (firewall/ACL, VPN-only, IP allowlist)
  • Stop or disable services that are not needed
  • Increase monitoring on the affected host until the fix lands

Record the mitigation, the owner and a target date. A mitigated finding that nobody revisits quietly becomes a permanent one.

Reference sources worth wiring into your workflow

  • CVE — common identifiers for publicly known vulnerabilities, used to match findings against vendor advisories.
  • CVSS (FIRST) — standardized severity scoring; useful, but context-free by design.
  • CIS Benchmarks — configuration hardening recommendations for OSes, server software, network devices and cloud services. Note that a CIS-based configuration audit is not automatically part of every platform assessment; ask if you need it.
  • JVN / IPA — vulnerability information for products used in Japan, handy if your stack includes Japanese vendor software.

Cloud is a scoping trap

Cloud VMs can be assessed much like on-prem servers, but two caveats apply. First, check the provider's terms and the shared responsibility boundary before testing. Second, assessing a VM is not the same as reviewing the cloud account's configuration — IAM permissions, storage exposure and similar settings are often a separate scope. Make sure everyone agrees which one is being bought.

Make it continuous

Infrastructure drifts. New hosts appear, configs change, a critical CVE drops on a Tuesday. Practical triggers for a re-assessment:

  • Before a new system goes live
  • After significant configuration or architecture changes
  • When a serious vulnerability affecting your stack is published

And keep expectations honest: an assessment reduces risk, it does not guarantee that every vulnerability was found or that future attacks will fail. It works alongside patching, access control, log monitoring and backups — not instead of them.

Further reading

If you want the full picture — the seven assessment areas, assessment methods, the six-step process, cost drivers and how to choose a provider — SotaTek Japan has a detailed Japanese-language write-up: Platform Vulnerability Assessment: 7 check areas, cost and methods.

TL;DR

  • Platform assessment covers the layer your web app pentest doesn't: OS, middleware, ports, network devices, TLS, config.
  • Scope deliberately: external vs. internal, authenticated vs. not, automated vs. manually verified.
  • Scanner output is raw data. Triage with exposure, exploitation and business impact — not CVSS alone.
  • Track interim mitigations, re-test after fixes, and re-assess when the platform changes.

Not everything can be fixed this sprint. Legacy dependencies, vendor appliances and change freezes are real. Interim mitigations are legitimate and should be tracked as such:

  • Restrict access to the vulnerable service (firewall/ACL, VPN-only, IP allowlist)
  • Stop or disable services that are not needed
  • Increase monitoring on the affected host until the fix lands

Record the mitigation, the owner and a target date. A mitigated finding that nobody revisits quietly becomes a permanent one.

Reference sources worth wiring into your workflow

  • CVE — common identifiers for publicly known vulnerabilities, used to match findings against vendor advisories.
  • CVSS (FIRST) — standardized severity scoring; useful, but context-free by design.
  • CIS Benchmarks — configuration hardening recommendations for OSes, server software, network devices and cloud services. Note that a CIS-based configuration audit is not automatically part of every platform assessment; ask if you need it.
  • JVN / IPA — vulnerability information for products used in Japan, handy if your stack includes Japanese vendor software.

Cloud is a scoping trap

Cloud VMs can be assessed much like on-prem servers, but two caveats apply. First, check the provider's terms and the shared responsibility boundary before testing. Second, assessing a VM is not the same as reviewing the cloud account's configuration — IAM permissions, storage exposure and similar settings are often a separate scope. Make sure everyone agrees which one is being bought.

Make it continuous

Infrastructure drifts. New hosts appear, configs change, a critical CVE drops on a Tuesday. Practical triggers for a re-assessment:

  • Before a new system goes live
  • After significant configuration or architecture changes
  • When a serious vulnerability affecting your stack is published

And keep expectations honest: an assessment reduces risk, it does not guarantee that every vulnerability was found or that future attacks will fail. It works alongside patching, access control, log monitoring and backups — not instead of them.

Further reading

If you want the full picture — the seven assessment areas, assessment methods, the six-step process, cost drivers and how to choose a provider — SotaTek Japan has a detailed Japanese-language write-up: Platform Vulnerability Assessment: 7 check areas, cost and methods.

TL;DR

  • Platform assessment covers the layer your web app pentest doesn't: OS, middleware, ports, network devices, TLS, config.
  • Scope deliberately: external vs. internal, authenticated vs. not, automated vs. manually verified.
  • Scanner output is raw data. Triage with exposure, exploitation and business impact — not CVSS alone.
  • Track interim mitigations, re-test after fixes, and re-assess when the platform changes.

title: An UNKNOWN that kept the wrong reason
summary:
Mishe watches its own parts with small checks. Each check runs on a timer, writes a verdict into a signal (GREEN, RED or UNKNOWN), and a dashboard shows the signal with its reason. A check can also say "I cannot tell": its input is stale or missing, so it declares UNKNOWN rather than a false GREEN. That is the right behaviour. The reason shown next to the UNKNOWN is where it went wrong.

Two repairs in one week, both small, both found by reading the dashboard instead of the code.

The reason that never updated

A check that could not observe would exit with a declared "unknown" code. The runner did the right thing with the signal: it marked it UNKNOWN. But when the signal was already UNKNOWN, the runner left the old reason in place. The old reason was whatever the signal had recorded first, something like "expired after 900s without observation", which is true about the age of the last reading and says nothing about why the check is failing now.

So the dashboard said the input had gone stale, when the check had written a precise cause into its own detail file: which device had not reported, and why. The runner read that file only to log it, and never copied the cause into the signal.

The fix is one rule. An already-UNKNOWN signal takes the check's own brief detail as its reason. A fresh GREEN still ages out to UNKNOWN as declared, so nothing that really went stale is hidden.

The reason that changed every five minutes

The first fix introduced the second bug. The check's detail contained ages and epoch counters, for example "last report 312s ago". Every five-minute run produced a slightly different string, so every run rewrote the reason. Subscribers were woken by an edge that meant nothing: the cause had not changed, only the number in it.

The repair compares causes with the digits removed. A repeated identical cause writes nothing. A genuinely new cause is still an edge.

The removal used a regular expression at first, and the repository has a rule that forbids regular expressions outside approved parsing adapters. The continuous integration run went red on that commit for the one reason the rule exists. The replacement is a plain loop that collapses runs of digits. The tests for the comparison did not change and still pass.

What to take from it

  • An UNKNOWN is an observation, and it needs a reason as true as a GREEN one. Age is not a cause.
  • Comparing a status by its text makes noise unless you strip the parts that move on every run. Decide what counts as a change before you write the comparison.
  • A rule written for a reason ("keep parsing at the boundary") is easy to break in a one-line fix. The check that enforces it is what caught it, not a reviewer.

These fixes are in the running release now. The next time a check goes UNKNOWN, the dashboard should say why, and it should not rewrite its reason every five minutes. If it does one or the other, that is a bug, and the reading that shows it is on the dashboard.

title: Scrapy proxy setup: middleware, rotation and retry rules
summary:
Originally published on proxymint.

Set a Scrapy proxy with meta or a middleware, then fix what breaks: tunnels that pin one exit, 407 TunnelErrors, per-domain concurrency and retries.

TL;DR

  • A Scrapy proxy is one meta key. Set request.meta["proxy"] to http://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT, or set it on every request from a downloader middleware at priority 350. The built-in HttpProxyMiddleware does the rest.
  • Kept-alive tunnels pin the exit. Scrapy reuses CONNECT tunnels for HTTPS, and every request inside one tunnel leaves from the same IP. In a local lab, 20 requests at template settings used 1 tunnel; a Connection: close header gave 20.
  • A 407 on an HTTPS page is a TunnelError, retried twice. TunnelError is in the default retry list, so bad credentials cost three attempts per URL. On a plain http:// page the 407 is a response that is dropped after one attempt.
  • CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_IP is deprecated and never meant the proxy. It keyed limits on the target's resolved IP. Scrapy 2.14.0 deprecated it; per-domain limits and AutoThrottle are what protect the site.
  • Scrapy retries 429 at once and ignores Retry-After. A small middleware that raises the domain's delay and retries once turns rate-limit responses into a slower crawl instead of extra traffic.

Key takeaways

  • Build the proxy URL in a middleware from environment variables. Encode username and password with quote(value, safe=""), keep the scheme http:// for every page, and use setdefault so a spider can still override it.
  • Choose reuse or a new exit per request on purpose. Leave keep-alive on for sessions; with a per-request rotation order, add Connection: close so every page opens its own tunnel, and accept a TLS handshake per page for it.
  • Run the 20-request exit check before a long crawl. Count distinct IPs from an IP echo endpoint with and without Connection: close, so rotation is measured rather than assumed.
  • Take 429 and 503 out of RETRY_HTTP_CODES. Handle them with a slow-down middleware, keep 403 and challenge pages out of every retry list, and stop when a site refuses the crawl.
  • Track MB per 1,000 items from downloader/response_bytes. Compare it across settings changes, and turn on HTTPCACHE_ENABLED during development so repeat runs move no proxy traffic.

Read the full guide on proxymint, with the commands, tables and sources.

title: AI deployment: from one graphics card to a team service
summary:
AI deployment: from one graphics card to a team service

From a demo to a service

AI deployment is the work that turns a model running on one machine into a service your team can rely on. Someone on your team has a model answering questions on one computer. It works, and people want to use it. Now you have to make it something the whole team can call from their own tools, every day.

This guide is for the manager who owns that request. It names the steps between the demo and the service and asks who owns each one. You do not need to choose any software to use it. You need to know what each step is for, so that you can ask the right person about it.

First, check that you need this

Running a model yourself is one way to give your team AI. A hosted AI product on a business plan can do the same job with less to run. So can a model you call through your cloud provider, and either is often easier.

If your data may leave your own machines under a contract your security team accepts, start there. That answer does not involve us. Read on if your data must stay on machines you control, or if the model you need is only available to download and run yourself.

The steps of an AI deployment

On one machine you already have a model that does the task. These are the parts around it that turn it into a service. We add them in this order.

  • An engine that serves requests An inference engine is the program that loads the model onto the graphics card and answers requests. A desktop tool serves one person at a time. A serving engine serves many people and programs calling it at once. Several good free engines exist. Our own setup uses one of these free serving engines, so many people can use the model at once. Its own documentation calls it fast and easy to use. Source: vLLM documentation, read on 14 November 2026. serve

  • A front door with keys A gateway is a program that every request passes through before it reaches the engine. It checks a key on every request, so only your own people and programs can use the model. Each team or tool gets its own key, and you can take one away without touching the others. The engine's own guide says that the simple key built into the engine is not enough, on its own, to keep strangers out. Source: vLLM documentation, running vLLM as a server, read on 14 November 2026. Our setup puts a gateway in front of the engine to check each key. The gateway's own guide says its key check lets you ask for a key before anyone reaches the services behind it. Source: Kong, Key Auth plugin, read on 14 November 2026. protect

  • A way to pull models, at a fixed version Teams download open models from a public library, most often Hugging Face. Hugging Face's own guide says that unless you name a version, you get the newest one. Source: Hugging Face, download files from the Hub, read on 14 November 2026. A service should pull the exact version you tested, so that the answers your users get do not change until someone decides to change them. lock the version

  • One machine first Run the engine, the gateway and the model puller together on one machine, called a host, before you plan for more. One host is simpler to secure, to watch and to fix. It also shows you how many people one machine can serve with your model. That is the fact you need before anyone talks about buying a second one. start small

  • A check before every change Over time you will get new model versions, engine updates and driver updates. A driver is the software that runs the graphics card. Each one can change how fast answers come, or what they say. Keep a short list of your own questions with answers you trust. Run it before each change reaches your users, and keep the old version until the new one passes. test

  • Someone named to keep it running A service needs a person who gets an alert when it stops. That person decides when to update it and answers when a user says it is slow. Name that person before the team depends on it, whether they are on your staff or someone you pay. own

Who owns each step

Write a name next to each step. In most teams the engine, the model puller, the host and the check before each change belong to one engineer, or to a small group. The gateway and its keys belong to that engineer together with your security team, who decide who may get a key. The person who keeps it running may be the same engineer. If so, say how much of their week it takes.

Two more people have to say yes. The person who owns the budget pays for the machine and the time. Security, legal or purchasing decide whether the service may touch real data. Bring both in before the pilot grows, not after. A service that works but that security never approved does not reach your users.

Agree what reliable means before you start

"Something the team can rely on" means different things to different people. Write down the answers to these questions, and agree them with the person who asked for the service.

  • Who uses it, and how many at once A tool for five engineers and a service behind a customer form are different services. The number of people calling it at the same time decides much of the rest. users

  • How long an answer may take Agree a wait that your users will accept, measured on your own machine with your own questions. Measure it today, before you change anything, so that you can judge every later change against it. speed

  • What happens when it is down Decide whether the team can wait, or whether work stops. If work stops, you need a plan for that from the start, and it changes what you build. outage

  • What it may see, and what you keep Decide which data your team may send to it, and whether you keep questions and answers, for how long, and who may read them. Your security team will ask about each of these. data

Where we fit

We are LLM Turnkey. We specialise in inference engine tuning, with support of Platform Alchemist's research and technology. Tuning means changing the engine's settings for how fast it answers and how many people it serves at once. Our starting setup is one command. It starts the engine, the gateway that checks keys and a tool that downloads models, all on one machine. It covers the first four steps above. Beyond this starting setup, we set up the engine for the AI model you use, on the hardware you own or rent. Then we tune it for speed and for the number of people it serves. We measure before and after on your own machines.

We are measuring our own setups now, and we will publish each result with its full setup.

title: Best Runbook Automation Tools in 2026: Semaphore, Rundeck, AWX, Windmill, and Ansible Automation Platform
summary:
Pick Semaphore for a lightweight, self-hosted UI that runs Ansible, Terraform, OpenTofu, Bash, and Python tasks. Pick AWX or Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform when you need centralized, governed Ansible at enterprise scale. Pick Rundeck (or its commercial edition, PagerDuty Process Automation) for general-purpose, multi-step runbooks with node targeting and fine-grained ACLs. Pick Windmill when runbooks blend into scripts, APIs, and internal tools. This guide compares the five tools on automation support, workflows, access control, and deployment effort.

What Is Runbook Automation?

Runbook automation tools help teams turn repetitive operational tasks into reusable workflows that can be executed consistently. Instead of manually connecting to servers, running commands, and following the same troubleshooting steps each time, teams can define these procedures once and make them available through a central interface. This can reduce repetitive work and make operational tasks easier to manage across teams.

What Are the Top Runbook Automation Tools?

Here are the top runbook automation tools in no specific order.

1. Semaphore

Semaphore is a self-hosted web interface and API for running automation. It supports Ansible, Terraform, OpenTofu, Terragrunt, Bash, PowerShell, and Python, allowing different types of automation to be managed from the same interface. It organizes automation around concepts such as Projects, Inventories, Task Templates, credentials, variables, and tasks. Users can run automation on demand or schedule it, while execution logs and task history provide visibility into what was executed.

One of Semaphore's main characteristics is its relatively lightweight architecture. It is written in Go and can be run as a single binary or container, with support for SQLite, MySQL, and PostgreSQL as its database backends. Tasks can execute directly on the Semaphore server or through runners placed closer to the systems being managed. It also provides a REST API for integrating automation into other systems and supports features such as credential management, scheduling, and CI/CD integration.

2. Rundeck

Rundeck is a general-purpose runbook automation platform designed to turn operational procedures into reusable jobs. Unlike Semaphore, it is not specifically tied to Ansible and can execute commands, scripts, and workflows across different types of infrastructure. Jobs can be triggered from the web interface, API, CLI, or on a schedule, and can target specific nodes using node filters.

A Rundeck job can contain multiple steps and supports workflow controls such as conditional execution, error handling, and different execution strategies. It also provides access control through ACL policies, secure credential storage through Key Storage, and execution history and audit information. Its plugin ecosystem allows it to integrate with platforms and services such as AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, ServiceNow, and PagerDuty.

Rundeck is available as an open-source product, while PagerDuty Process Automation provides the commercial offering around Rundeck and other automation capabilities. The commercial offering adds features aimed at organizations that need centralized administration, enterprise integrations, access controls, and support. This makes Rundeck and PagerDuty Process Automation suitable for teams that need a broader runbook automation platform with more advanced workflow and enterprise management capabilities.

3. AWX

AWX is the open-source upstream project associated with Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform and provides a web-based interface and API for managing Ansible automation. It adds a management layer around Ansible rather than requiring users to execute playbooks directly from the command line. Automation can be organized through inventories, projects, credentials, job templates, and workflows, while users can monitor execution and review the output of completed jobs.

AWX is particularly focused on managing Ansible at a larger scale. It provides features such as role-based access control, job scheduling, workflow automation, and centralized management of inventories and credentials. Because of the number of components and capabilities involved, its deployment is more involved than a lightweight tool such as Semaphore. It is generally aimed at environments where Ansible is already an important part of the automation stack and where centralized management and team-level controls are important.

4. Windmill

Windmill is a broader automation and internal-tools platform rather than a runbook tool built specifically around infrastructure automation. It allows users to turn scripts into executable jobs, APIs, scheduled tasks, workflows, and user-facing applications. It supports a wide range of languages and technologies, including Python, TypeScript, Go, Bash, PowerShell, SQL, Docker, and Ansible. Scripts can be created through its web interface or developed locally and then deployed to Windmill.

The main building block in Windmill is the Script, which can be executed independently or combined with other scripts into a Flow. Flows can include dependencies, branches, loops, approvals, webhooks, and scheduled execution, making the platform useful for more complex workflows. Ansible is supported as one of the script types, so existing Ansible automation can also be brought into the platform. This broader approach makes Windmill suitable for teams that want to combine infrastructure automation with application-level workflows and internal tools.

5. Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform

Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform is the enterprise automation platform built around Ansible. It provides a collection of components for developing, managing, executing, and scaling automation across an organization. One of its central components is Automation Controller, which provides a web interface and API for managing inventories, launching jobs, scheduling workflows, controlling access, and tracking automation activity.

The platform goes beyond simply providing a UI for Ansible playbooks. It includes capabilities for managing automation content, executing automation across different environments, creating workflows, integrating with CI/CD systems, and scaling execution through Automation Mesh. Current versions also include components such as Automation Hub and Event-Driven Ansible, which extend the platform into content management and event-based automation. Because it is designed for enterprise environments, it provides a much broader set of capabilities than lightweight Ansible interfaces.

Which Runbook Automation Tool Is Best for Your Team?

There is no single runbook automation tool that is the best fit for every team. The right choice depends on the type of automation, the level of control required, and how much infrastructure the team wants around the automation.

For Ansible-focused automation, Semaphore, AWX, and Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform are the closest options. Semaphore keeps things lightweight and provides a simple interface for running and managing Ansible automation, while AWX adds more centralized management and enterprise-style controls. Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform builds further on this with additional enterprise features, governance, and scaling capabilities.

For general-purpose runbook automation, Rundeck and PagerDuty Process Automation are more closely aligned. They are not tied to Ansible and can run commands, scripts, and multi-step workflows across different systems. They also provide stronger workflow controls, node targeting, access management, and integrations.

Windmill sits somewhat outside the traditional runbook category. It supports scripts and workflows across multiple languages and can turn them into jobs, APIs, schedules, and internal tools. title: Reliable JSON from LLMs: From Prompting to Constrained Decoding
summary:
If you have built an AI agent that interfaces with standard backend APIs, you have likely encountered this failure mode: your parser expects a raw JSON payload, but the model returns Sure! Here is the JSON output you requested: followed by markdown blocks.

In a sandbox, this is a minor annoyance. In a production pipeline processing thousands of automated calls per day, an unhandled parsing exception breaks downstream services, creates invalid database entries, and inflates your error logs.

Prompting an LLM to "return only valid JSON" usually achieves 80% to 95% reliability. While that sounds acceptable, a 5% to 20% failure rate in automated backend workflows means constant human intervention and fragile code.

To build deterministic workflows on top of non-deterministic models, we need to understand how JSON extraction has evolved—and how to enforce structural guarantees.

The Three Levels of JSON Extraction

Getting structured data from LLMs generally falls into three paradigms, each offering different levels of reliability.

1. System Prompting

You instruct the model inside the system prompt: "Return only raw JSON matching key 'user_id' as an integer."

  • The Problem: Models easily forget instructions under high context loads, hallucinate extra explanatory text, or use single quotes instead of double quotes. It provides zero static type guarantees.

2. Native Function / Tool Calling

You supply a JSON Schema inside the API call, framing the output as a function argument call.

  • The Problem: While significantly better than prompting, the model can still emit incorrect data types (e.g., returning a string "123" where an integer 123 is required) or omit required fields when dealing with edge cases.

3. Constrained Decoding (Grammar-Based Sampling)

Instead of letting the model freely pick tokens and hoping it respects your schema, constrained decoding intervenes at the sampling layer.

During token generation, the runtime masks out any token logits that would violate the context-free grammar of your JSON schema. The model is physically incapable of emitting a character that violates your schema structure. It cannot output introductory text, wrong types, or missing required keys.

Implementing Strict Schema Enforcement

Modern LLM provider APIs and local inference engines (like vLLM or Ollama) now support constrained decoding natively.

Here is how to enforce strict JSON schemas using Python, Pydantic, and OpenAI's structured outputs engine:

from typing import List
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

# Define the exact contract for your backend pipeline
class SystemMetricsReport(BaseModel):
    hostname: str
    cpu_usage_percent: float
    active_services: List[str]
    requires_maintenance: bool = Field(
        description="True if CPU exceeds 85% or critical services are down"
    )

def extract_metrics(unstructured_log: str) -> SystemMetricsReport:
    completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
        model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "system", 
                "content": "Extract server health metrics from log dumps."
            },
            {"role": "user", "content": unstructured_log},
        ],
        response_format=SystemMetricsReport,
    )

    # Returns an instantiated Pydantic object, completely validated
    return completion.choices[0].message.parsed

If you run open-weight models on your own infrastructure (e.g., using vLLM or Outlines), you can apply guided decoding to achieve the exact same behavior locally:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from outlines import models, generate

# Load local model
model = models.transformers("mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2")

class DatabaseQuery(BaseModel):
    table: str
    limit: int

# Build a constrained generator bound strictly to the Pydantic schema
generator = generate.json(model, DatabaseQuery)
result = generator("Fetch top 10 users from the database")

# Guaranteed to be a valid DatabaseQuery instance
print(result.table, result.limit)

Backend and DevOps Considerations

When moving constrained decoding into production, keep these operational details in mind:

  1. Schema Rejection vs. Generation Errors: If the model cannot satisfy both the prompt instructions and the schema constraints, it will fail at generation time rather than returning invalid data. Ensure your API wrappers catch schema validation errors gracefully.
  2. Token Latency: Constrained decoding adds a small overhead during logit masking, but it eliminates the latency overhead of multi-turn retries or JSON fixup loops.
  3. Decouple Logic: Always pass validated Pydantic models directly into your business logic rather than raw dictionaries. This preserves type safety across your entire microservice boundary.

Relying on system prompts for JSON formatting is a technical debt risk in automated systems. By enforcing constrained decoding at the sampling layer, your AI agents become as deterministic as traditional API endpoints.

title: Ubuntu 26.04 golden images on Hetzner with cloud-init
summary:
Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud

The snapshot your team has cloned for two years was built by hand on Ubuntu 24.04. Nobody remembers which packages went in, the user-data file has grown to 200 lines, and the first reboot of every new server runs a slow apt upgrade. Ubuntu 26.04 golden images are the cleanest way to reset that, and the timing is right. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released on 2026-04-23, and its first point release, 26.04.1, is now out. Historically, the first point release is when Canonical opens LTS-to-LTS upgrades, and many teams wait for it before treating an LTS as safe for fleets.

Short answer: build a fresh 26.04 snapshot with Packer's hcloud builder instead of upgrading old snapshots. Bake slow, stable things (packages, hardening, agents) into the image. Leave per-server things (users, keys, hostnames) to cloud-init user-data at first boot. This applies to Hetzner Cloud fleets. If you install from ISO or on dedicated hardware, the autoinstall section below is the relevant path.

What changed and who is affected

Two mechanisms get confused here:

  • cloud-init configures an already-installed image at boot. This is what Hetzner Cloud uses.
  • Autoinstall is the Subiquity installer's unattended mode for installing Ubuntu from ISO. It uses an autoinstall.yaml with autoinstall: version: 1 and can embed a cloud-init user-data section.

Hetzner Cloud servers start from provider images or your snapshots. Autoinstall therefore matters only if you install from ISO, use a rescue-and-install flow, or run dedicated servers.

You are affected if any of these is true:

  • Your servers boot from a hand-made 24.04 snapshot that was never cleaned with cloud-init clean.
  • Your user-data installs packages at every boot, so scaling out is slow and depends on mirror availability.
  • Your provisioning scripts assume specific userland behavior, such as sudo flags or GNU coreutils output parsing. Recent Ubuntu releases have moved some core utilities toward Rust implementations. Check the 26.04 release notes against your scripts rather than assuming parity.

Cost: a snapshot is billed per GB per month, and you will hold at least two (old and new) during the migration. Treat the exact Hetzner image name for 26.04 as something to verify, not assume (see step 1).

Before/after config

The "before" pattern does everything at boot, on every server. It is slow and non-deterministic because it depends on the mirror state at that moment.

#cloud-config
# BEFORE: everything happens at first boot, on every server
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
packages: [fail2ban, unattended-upgrades, prometheus-node-exporter]
runcmd:
  - [sh, -c, "curl -fsSL https://example.com/harden.sh | sh"]  # unpinned, unaudited

🧪 Lab — try this in your browser

  • EOL Countdown — Check when your Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Node.js, Ubuntu… versions lose support. Paste command output or add versions — get status, days left and calendar reminders.

The "after" split keeps the slow work in the image and shrinks user-data to identity and secrets. This is the Packer template (HCL2) for the image:

packer {
  required_plugins {
    hcloud = {
      source  = "github.com/hetznercloud/hcloud"
      version = ">= 1.6.0"   # check the plugin releases for the current version
    }
  }
}

variable "hcloud_token" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
variable "server_type"  { type = string }   # pick from: hcloud server-type list

locals {
  build_ts = formatdate("YYYYMMDDhhmm", timestamp())
}

source "hcloud" "golden" {
  token         = var.hcloud_token
  image         = "ubuntu-26.04"            # verify: hcloud image list --type system
  location      = "fsn1"
  server_type   = var.server_type
  ssh_username  = "root"
  snapshot_name = "golden-ubuntu-2604-${local.build_ts}"
  snapshot_labels = { role = "golden", os = "ubuntu-26.04" }
}

build {
  sources = ["source.hcloud.golden"]
  provisioner "shell" {
    inline = [
      "cloud-init status --wait",   # let first-boot cloud-init finish before changing things
      "apt-get update && DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y dist-upgrade",
      "DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y install fail2ban unattended-upgrades prometheus-node-exporter",
      "cloud-init clean --logs --seed",   # re-arm cloud-init for the next boot
      "truncate -s 0 /etc/machine-id",    # avoid duplicate machine IDs across clones
      "rm -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*"         # host keys are regenerated on first boot
    ]
  }
}

Step-by-step migration to Ubuntu 26.04 golden images

  1. Confirm the base image. Run hcloud image list --type system | grep -i ubuntu and use the exact name it prints. If 26.04 is missing in your project or location, stop here. Do not upgrade a 24.04 box in place instead.
  2. Move user-data to identity only. Remove package installs and hardening scripts. Keep users, SSH keys, hostname and write_files for per-environment config.
  3. Build. Inject the token from your secret store or CI secret as an environment variable, never in the template or on the command line: export PKR_VAR_hcloud_token="". Then run packer init . && packer build -var "server_type=" .
  4. Validate user-data against the schema before using it. Run cloud-init schema --config-file user-data.yaml on any machine with cloud-init installed. The slim file looks like this:
#cloud-config
hostname: web-01
ssh_pwauth: false
users:
  - name: deploy
    groups: [sudo]
    shell: /bin/bash
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"   # tighten if your policy requires a password
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... deploy@ci
  1. Canary first. Point one non-critical server at the new snapshot ID and keep the rest on the old one. Use the same workflow you already use for fleet changes (Ansible, OpenTofu or Terraform), so the image ID lives in one variable.
  2. Widen gradually by replacing servers, not upgrading them. Replacement is what makes rollback trivial.

If you do need autoinstall for ISO or dedicated installs, keep the same split:

  • A minimal autoinstall.yaml for identity, SSH and storage layout.
  • Everything else in the embedded user-data.

The Subiquity documentation lists the current schema. Field names and defaults are version-dependent.

Verify and roll back

Create a throwaway server from the new snapshot. Check that cloud-init ran as a first boot, not a replay of the build:

hcloud server create --name golden-test --type  \
  --image  --ssh-key deploy \
  --user-data-from-file user-data.yaml

ssh deploy@ 'cloud-init status --long; sudo cloud-init schema --system; \
  cat /etc/machine-id; ls /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*; lsb_release -ds'

Expect:

  • status: done with no errors.
  • A schema validation message saying the config is valid.
  • A freshly generated, non-empty machine ID that differs from the build host.
  • New SSH host keys.
  • An Ubuntu 26.04 description string.

Also check /var/log/cloud-init.log for warnings. To confirm time-to-ready improved, compare cloud-init analyze blame and systemd-analyze output with a server on the old image. Record your own numbers; do not trust anyone else's.

Rollback means replacing servers back onto the previous snapshot ID. That only works if you do not delete the old snapshot. Label it (for example role=golden-previous) and keep it for at least one full release cycle of your own services. Roll back on a concrete signal:

  • Failed health checks on canaries.
  • cloud-init status reporting error.
  • A regression in your application's package set.

The snapshot your team has cloned for two years was built by hand on Ubuntu 24.04. Nobody remembers which packages went in, the user-data file has grown to 200 lines, and the first reboot of every new server runs a slow apt upgrade. Ubuntu 26.04 golden images are the cleanest way to reset that, and the timing is right. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released on 2026-04-23, and its first point release, 26.04.1, is now out. Historically, the first point release is when Canonical opens LTS-to-LTS upgrades, and many teams wait for it before treating an LTS as safe for fleets.

What changed and who is affected

Two mechanisms get confused here:

  • cloud-init configures an already-installed image at boot. This is what Hetzner Cloud uses.
  • Autoinstall is the Subiquity installer's unattended mode for installing Ubuntu from ISO. It uses an autoinstall.yaml with autoinstall: version: 1 and can embed a cloud-init user-data section.

# BEFORE: everything happens at first boot, on every server

package_upgrade: true
packages: [fail2ban, unattended-upgrades, prometheus-node-exporter]
runcmd:
  - [sh, -c, "curl -fsSL https://example.com/harden.sh | sh"]  # unpinned, unaudited

packer {
  required_plugins {
    hcloud = {
      source  = "github.com/hetznercloud/hcloud"
      version = ">= 1.6.0"   # check the plugin releases for the current version
    }
  }
}

variable "hcloud_token" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
variable "server_type"  { type = string }   # pick from: hcloud server-type list

locals {
  build_ts = formatdate("YYYYMMDDhhmm", timestamp())
}

source "hcloud" "golden" {
  token         = var.hcloud_token
  image         = "ubuntu-26.04"            # verify: hcloud image list --type system
  location      = "fsn1"
  server_type   = var.server_type
  ssh_username  = "root"
  snapshot_name = "golden-ubuntu-2604-${local.build_ts}"
  snapshot_labels = { role = "golden", os = "ubuntu-26.04" }
}

build {
  sources = ["source.hcloud.golden"]
  provisioner "shell" {
    inline = [
      "cloud-init status --wait",   # let first-boot cloud-init finish before changing things
      "apt-get update && DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y dist-upgrade",
      "DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y install fail2ban unattended-upgrades prometheus-node-exporter",

hostname: web-01
ssh_pwauth: false

    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"   # tighten if your policy requires a password
    ssh_authorized_keys:

title: HTTP 413 Request Entity Too Large: nginx fix
summary:
The request body (usually an upload) is larger than the limit nginx or a proxy in front of it allows – the request never reaches the application.

Common causes

  • client_max_body_size is not set; the nginx default is 1 MB.
  • The directive is in the wrong context or in a file that is not included.
  • A second proxy in front (load balancer, Docker proxy, Cloudflare with 100 MB on the free plan) has its own limit.
  • PHP limits upload_max_filesize and post_max_size are too small (usually an application error rather than 413).

How to check it

Find the effective value in the loaded config

nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -n client_max_body_size

Find 413 cases in the log

grep 'too large body' /var/log/nginx/error.log | tail -n 10

Check the PHP-FPM limits (not the CLI ones)

grep -rE 'upload_max_filesize|post_max_size' /etc/php/8.3/fpm/

What actually helps

  1. Set client_max_body_size 10G; in the right server or location block (0 disables the check).
  2. Test and reload: nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx.
  3. Raise the same limit on every proxy in front.

FAQ

Why doesn't changing php.ini help?

Because the 413 comes from nginx before PHP ever sees the request. Also, PHP-FPM uses a different php.ini than the CLI.

Is client_max_body_size 0 a good idea?

Only behind authentication. On public endpoints it allows arbitrarily large requests and makes simple resource attacks easy.

Full page with every command and the German/Italian version: daniele-michelin.com/en/errors/http-413-request-entity-too-large/

First published at daniele-michelin.com. The error lexicon covers HTTP, DNS, TLS, mail, database, PHP, nginx, systemd and Nextcloud, in German, English and Italian.

title: A pre Black Friday monitoring checklist (do it this afternoon, not Thursday night)
summary:
Black Friday is coming up this Friday. Assuming you are running an online shop, or a SaaS that online shops depend on, this is the weekend when "the site was a bit slow for a while, or down" turns into lost revenue you can actually count.

Most of what goes wrong isn't exotic. It's a certificate that expired, a checkout that returns a friendly 200 while being broken, or an alert that went to someone who was asleep. Here's a checklist that takes an afternoon. Every item comes from a failure that has actually happened.

1. Things that expire

TLS certificates, on every hostname. That means www, shop., api., the checkout subdomain, the callback URLs your payment provider calls, and any custom domain on your CDN.

Two things changed recently that make this more likely to bite:

  • Since March 15, 2026, publicly trusted certificates are valid for at most 200 days (down from 398), and the limit drops to 100 days in March 2027. Renewals happen more often, so a broken renewal job shows up sooner.
  • Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry-warning emails in June 2025. If your renewal job quietly broke, nobody will tell you.

Check every hostname now:

for h in www.example.com shop.example.com api.example.com; do
  end=$(echo | openssl s_client -servername "$h" -connect "$h:443" 2>/dev/null \
        | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2)
  echo "$h -> $end"
done

Anything that expires before mid-December, renew it this week.

Domains. In 2017 Marketo forgot to renew marketo.com, and it took the site and its customers' tracking links down with it. If a company that size can do it, so can anyone.

whois example.com | grep -i expir

2. Monitor what makes money, not just /

A homepage check tells you the homepage works. Customers don't pay you on the homepage.

  • Cart, checkout and sign-up. Check each one for text that only renders when the page really works, such as "Order summary" or "Payment method". A cached page, a maintenance page or an error template can all return 200 OK. 
  curl -fsS https://shop.example.com/cart | grep -q "Order summary" \
    && echo "OK" || echo "BROKEN"
  • Every API the storefront depends on: stock, shipping rates, payments, search. Check your own health endpoint as well, and check what the body says, not only the status code.
  • Response time. Set a threshold. A checkout that takes 9 seconds is down for most shoppers, even though it's technically up. 
  curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'total: %{time_total}s\n' https://shop.example.com/checkout

3. The jobs nobody watches

Stock sync, price feeds, abandoned-cart emails, nightly backups: they run from cron or a scheduler, and when one stops, nothing turns red. You find out when a customer buys something you don't have.

Make each job report in when it finishes, and alert when the report doesn't arrive (a "heartbeat" or "dead man's switch" check):

# last line of the job: only runs if everything before it succeeded
/usr/local/bin/sync-stock.sh && curl -fsS -m 10 https://your-heartbeat-url >/dev/null

Set the expected interval a little longer than the job's schedule, and send the alert to the same on-call person as everything else.

4. Detect fast, without crying wolf

  • Shorten your check intervals for the weekend. Five minutes between checks is a long time when the checkout is down.
  • Confirm from a second location before alerting. A blip on one network path shouldn't wake anyone up at 3 a.m. If people learn to ignore alerts in November, they'll ignore the real one in December.

5. People

  • Write down who is on call from Thursday to Monday, with phone numbers, and make sure they know.
  • Set up escalation. If the first person doesn't acknowledge within N minutes, the alert goes to the next one. Holiday weekends are exactly when "I didn't see the notification" happens.

6. A change freeze

  • No deploys, no plugin updates, and automatic updates off from Wednesday.
  • Take a full backup, and test the restore. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a backup.

7. Communication

  • Have a status page, so customers can check whether it's you without opening a ticket. Every ticket you don't get is one less thing to answer while you're fixing the problem.
  • Write the message for "our hosting or CDN provider is down" now. You won't write a good one at 2 a.m.

When Fastly failed on June 8, 2021, one customer's valid config change triggered a latent bug, and 85% of Fastly's network returned errors. Every site on it went down at the same moment. You can't fix that kind of outage, but you can be the one who tells your customers first.

8. Know your providers' status pages, and don't rely on them

During the 2017 AWS S3 outage, AWS couldn't update its own status dashboard for about two hours, because the dashboard depended on S3. In June 2025, Google Cloud's status page lagged by about an hour for a similar reason.

Bookmark your providers' status pages, but your own external checks are what tell you first.

The short version

  • [ ] Every certificate is valid until mid-December or later
  • [ ] Domains are renewed, with auto-renew on
  • [ ] Cart, checkout, sign-up and APIs are monitored, with keyword checks
  • [ ] A response-time threshold is set
  • [ ] Every scheduled job reports in when it finishes
  • [ ] Shorter check intervals, with confirmation from a second location
  • [ ] On-call rota and escalation are written down
  • [ ] Change freeze from Wednesday, backup tested
  • [ ] Status page is ready, and the "provider is down" message is written

Got something to add to my list? Tell me in the comments.

2. Monitor what makes money, not just /

A homepage check tells you the homepage works. Customers don't pay you on the homepage.

  • Cart, checkout and sign-up. Check each one for text that only renders when the page really works, such as "Order summary" or "Payment method". A cached page, a maintenance page or an error template can all return 200 OK. 
  curl -fsS https://shop.example.com/cart | grep -q "Order summary" \
    && echo "OK" || echo "BROKEN"
  • Every API the storefront depends on: stock, shipping rates, payments, search. Check your own health endpoint as well, and check what the body says, not only the status code.
  • Response time. Set a threshold. A checkout that takes 9 seconds is down for most shoppers, even though it's technically up. 
  curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'total: %{time_total}s\n' https://shop.example.com/checkout

3. The jobs nobody watches

Stock sync, price feeds, abandoned-cart emails, nightly backups: they run from cron or a scheduler, and when one stops, nothing turns red. You find out when a customer buys something you don't have.

Make each job report in when it finishes, and alert when the report doesn't arrive (a "heartbeat" or "dead man's switch" check):

# last line of the job: only runs if everything before it succeeded
/usr/local/bin/sync-stock.sh && curl -fsS -m 10 https://your-heartbeat-url >/dev/null

Set the expected interval a little longer than the job's schedule, and send the alert to the same on-call person as everything else.

4. Detect fast, without crying wolf

  • Shorten your check intervals for the weekend. Five minutes between checks is a long time when the checkout is down.
  • Confirm from a second location before alerting. A blip on one network path shouldn't wake anyone up at 3 a.m. If people learn to ignore alerts in November, they'll ignore the real one in December.

5. People

  • Write down who is on call from Thursday to Monday, with phone numbers, and make sure they know.
  • Set up escalation. If the first person doesn't acknowledge within N minutes, the alert goes to the next one. Holiday weekends are exactly when "I didn't see the notification" happens.

6. A change freeze

  • No deploys, no plugin updates, and automatic updates off from Wednesday.
  • Take a full backup, and test the restore. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a backup.

7. Communication

  • Have a status page, so customers can check whether it's you without opening a ticket. Every ticket you don't get is one less thing to answer while you're fixing the problem.
  • Write the message for "our hosting or CDN provider is down" now. You won't write a good one at 2 a.m.

When Fastly failed on June 8, 2021, one customer's valid config change triggered a latent bug, and 85% of Fastly's network returned errors. Every site on it went down at the same moment. You can't fix that kind of outage, but you can be the one who tells your customers first.

8. Know your providers' status pages, and don't rely on them

During the 2017 AWS S3 outage, AWS couldn't update its own status dashboard for about two hours, because the dashboard depended on S3. In June 2025, Google Cloud's status page lagged by about an hour for a similar reason.

Bookmark your providers' status pages, but your own external checks are what tell you first.
